title: Assess with more than a few task types
statement: Assess with more than a few kinds of task, because what a test asks shapes what is taught and one usual format can narrow teaching to it.
detail: A reading project's research synthesis quotes the RAND Reading Study Group: assessments that are widely used today focus heavily on only a few tasks and thus may inadvertently limit the reading curriculum to preparation for those few tasks (p. xix) (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/reading-science/SYNTHESIS.qmd`). The same passage adds that while comprehension is defined by default as reading a passage and answering a few multiple-choice questions, there is little incentive to teach the deeper construct (p. 113). Never let one format, such as a passage with a few multiple-choice questions, become the definition of a skill.
against: It is a study group's argument from 2002, not a measurement. A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans-wiki/Perfect-Course-Rulebook.md`). A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans-wiki/Peter-Pan-Quality-Case-Study-2026-08-24.md`).

evidence.quote: "assessments that are widely used today focus heavily on only a few tasks and thus may inadvertently limit the reading curriculum to preparation for those few tasks."
as long as we define comprehension by default as reading a passage and answering a few multiple-choice questions about it,
the absence of attention to these consequences in widely used reading assessments diminishes the emphasis on them in instructional practices as well.

**114. Defaulting to 'read a passage, answer a few multiple-choice questions' as the operational definition of comprehension gives teachers little incentive to teach toward a deeper, more accurate conception of the construct.**

**124. No single assessment can satisfy all these requirements; the RFA instead calls for building an integrated system of multiple assessments serving different purposes (accountability, diagnosis, instruction-guidance) and different reader groups.**
Variety is not a quality goal. The same format can be excellent for one construct and invalid for another.
Variety for its own sake is noise.
Do not let single-select MCQ dominate; STAAR caps it at 75 percent of points and the 2026-06-29 build was at about 87 percent.
"about 87 percent of items are single-select multiple choice, STAAR's inline-choice and text-entry item types are missing, and at least one item is mistagged."

But about 87 percent of items are single-select multiple choice, STAAR’s inline-choice and text-entry item types are missing, and at least one item is mistagged (a vocabulary item labelled Inference and Evidence), which weakens the claim of full standards alignment.

citations.ref: RAND Reading Study Group 2002, Reading for Understanding: Toward an R&D Program in Reading Comprehension (MR-1465)
